title: Kinetic theory of gases; Temperature, internal energy, thermal equilibrium
source: Questions copied unchanged from the mission-lesson scripts for Eduqas A-level Physics (status of the source: mission-lesson scripts of Oct-Nov 2026 (reviewed by AI reviewers; not signed off by a person)). Terms and clues: T06-1#t4 term and clue written for the game; T06-1#t2 term and clue written for the game; T06-1#t3 term and clue written for the game; T06-1#t1 term and clue written for the game. Questions: T01-1#N.2, T06-1#N.4a, T06-uk1#N.6, T01-1#N.5, T06-1#N.8a, T06-uk1#N.8, T01-1#N.9a, T06-1#N.14, T06-uk1#N.11, T01-1#N.11.

assemble.prompt: Match each term to its definition.

items.label: Elastic collision
items.clue: Impact between particles, or with a wall, in which no kinetic energy is lost.

items.label: rms speed
items.clue: Measure of molecular motion giving 408 m s⁻¹, not the plain average 400, for 300, 400 and 500 m s⁻¹.

items.label: Internal energy
items.clue: Total random kinetic plus potential contributions of the particles; depends only on T in this model.

items.label: Ideal gas
items.clue: Model: a huge number of particles in rapid random motion, of negligible volume, with forces only in impacts.

questions.stem: A 0.20 kg copper block at 80 °C is lowered into a large tank containing 200 kg of water at 20 °C. The water has far more internal energy than the block. Which statement describes the resultant thermal energy transfer?

options.text: From the block to the water, until they reach the same temperature.
From the water to the block, since the water has more internal energy.
Coldness passes from the water into the block, so the block cools down.
From the block to the water, until they have equal internal energies.

questions.stem: A sealed, rigid container of ideal gas is heated. What happens to the pressure of the gas, and why?

options.text: It rises: the molecules expand when they are heated, so they strike the walls more often.
It stays the same: the number of molecules per unit volume has not changed at all.
It rises: faster molecules hit the walls more often, each with a greater change in momentum.
It rises: the molecules collide more often with one another, and so push harder on the walls.

questions.stem: Nitrogen in a cylinder has a density of 3.40 kg m⁻³. The root-mean-square speed of its molecules is 517 m s⁻¹. Treat it as an ideal gas. What is its pressure?

options.text: 586 Pa

questions.explanation: p = ⅓ρ × (mean square speed) = ⅓ × 3.40 × 517² = 3.03 × 10⁵ Pa.

questions.stem: Sample P is warmed from 10 °C to 30 °C. Sample Q is warmed from 290 K to 310 K. Which statement about the two temperature changes is correct?

options.text: P's rise of 20 °C is equivalent to a rise of 293 K.
The changes differ, since kelvins and °C differ in size.
Both undergo the same temperature change, 20 K.
P's rise is larger, since P's temperature tripled.

questions.stem: A sealed container of gas is heated from 27 °C to 177 °C. By what factor does the mean kinetic energy of the gas molecules increase?
questions.explanation: T rises from 300 K to 450 K. Mean kinetic energy ∝ T, so it rises by 450/300 = 1.5.

questions.stem: An ideal gas is heated from 27 °C to 927 °C. By what factor does the rms speed of its molecules increase?
questions.explanation: ½m(rms speed)² ∝ T, so rms speed ∝ √T. √(1200/300) = √4 = 2.0.

questions.stem: You have 1.0 kg of ice at 0 °C and 1.0 kg of liquid water at 0 °C. Which statement about their internal energies is correct?

options.text: They are equal, since both are at the same temperature.
The water has more: its molecules have more potential energy.
The ice has more, since strong forces hold its molecules in place.
The water has more, since its molecules move faster on average.

questions.explanation: Melting takes in energy with no rise in temperature. That energy separates the molecules, raising their potential energy; their mean kinetic energy is unchanged.

questions.stem: A container holds a mixture of hydrogen (H₂) and oxygen (O₂) at one temperature. An oxygen molecule has 16 times the mass of a hydrogen molecule. What is (rms speed of the hydrogen molecules)/(rms speed of the oxygen molecules)?

options.text: 1, because the two gases are at the same temperature.
16, because the hydrogen molecules have 1/16 of the mass.
1/4, because the heavier molecules hit harder and so move faster.
4, because equal mean kinetic energies mean speed ∝ 1/√m.

questions.explanation: ½m(rms speed)², the mean kinetic energy, depends only on T, so it is the same for both, so rms speed ∝ 1/√m = √16 = 4.

questions.stem: Two sealed containers of equal volume are at the same temperature. Each holds the same number N of molecules of an ideal gas. Each molecule of gas Y has 4 times the mass of a molecule of gas X. What is (pressure of Y)/(pressure of X)?

options.text: 4, because pV = ⅓Nm × (mean square speed) and m is 4 times as large.
1, because m × (mean square speed) is the same for both gases at the same temperature.
¼, because the heavier molecules move more slowly and hit the walls less often.
2, because the molecules of Y have half the rms speed and 4 times the mass.

questions.explanation: Same T → same mean translational KE, so m × (mean square speed) is equal. With equal N and V, pV = ⅓Nm × (mean square speed) gives equal pressures (as pV = NkT says).

questions.stem: A thermometer at room temperature, 20 °C, is placed in a cup of water at 70 °C. Its reading rises for a while and then stays steady. Why does the steady reading give the temperature of the water?

options.text: All energy transfer between the thermometer and the water has then stopped completely for good.
The thermometer then has as much internal energy as the water in the cup, so the two readings match.
The cold in the thermometer has then all flowed out into the water, so it can read correctly.
They are then in thermal equilibrium, so no net energy is transferred between them.
